title: CIDR Notation and Subnetting
intro: Every VPC, subnet, security group rule, and Kubernetes pod network is defined in CIDR notation. Being able to reason about ranges quickly prevents overlapping networks — a mistake that's painful to undo later.

steps.prompt: Show the details of the 10.0.0.0/16 range your VPC will use.
steps.explanation: /16 means the first 16 bits are fixed; the remaining 16 give 65,534 usable addresses.
steps.why: Each step up in the prefix halves the size: /16 = 65k, /24 = 256, /28 = 16. Cloud providers also reserve a few addresses per subnet (AWS reserves 5), so a /28 only gives you 11 usable IPs.

steps.prompt: Check what range 10.0.1.0/24 covers — one of the subnets you'll carve out of the VPC.
steps.why: Splitting a VPC into /24s gives 256 non-overlapping subnets, a common simple scheme (e.g. public subnets 10.0.0-2.0/24, private 10.0.10-12.0/24, one per availability zone).

steps.prompt: Check whether the office VPN range 10.0.128.0/17 would overlap with the VPC.
steps.why: Overlapping ranges can't be routed between: with a VPN or VPC peering, traffic for an overlapping address has no way to know which side to go to. This is why choosing non-overlapping ranges up front (across every VPC, office, and pod network) matters so much.

steps.prompt: Check the default Kubernetes pod network range many clusters use, 10.244.0.0/16, against your VPC's 10.0.0.0/16.
steps.explanation: 10.244.x.x doesn't overlap 10.0.x.x — safe to use alongside this VPC.
steps.why: Pod CIDR, Service CIDR, VPC CIDR, and any peered or VPN networks must ALL be mutually non-overlapping. The pod CIDR is set at cluster creation (see kubeadm init --pod-network-cidr) and is very hard to change afterwards.
